examples.knowledge_point: Applying De Moivre's Theorem to Fractions
examples.worked_solution:
First, note that

$$
\dfrac{1}{\left[ \cos(\theta) +\textrm{i}\sin(\theta) \right]^2} = \left[ \cos(\theta) +\textrm{i}\sin(\theta) \right]^{-2} .
$$

De Moivre's Theorem states that

$$
\left[ \cos(\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin(\varphi) \right]^n = \cos(n\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin{(n\varphi)}.
$$

In our expression, we have $n=-2$ and $\varphi=\theta.$ Substituting in these values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )]}^{2}} & ={[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )]}^{-2} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2\theta )+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the fact that $\cos(-\varphi) = \cos (\varphi)$ and $\sin(-\varphi) = -\sin(\varphi)$ for any input $\varphi,$ we have

$$
\cos(-2\theta) + \textrm{i}\sin(-2\theta) = \cos(2\theta) - \textrm{i}\sin{(2\theta)}.
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
De Moivre's Theorem states that

$$
[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\phi )+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\phi )]^{n}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\phi )+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\phi ).
$$

In our expression, we have $n=10$ and $\phi =\theta .$ Substituting in these values, we get

$$
[\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]^{10}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(10\theta )+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10\theta ).
$$
